I’d replace **“Revert to here”** with **“Restore model version…”**, shown only beside a timeline event that has a saved model version. A chat turn by itself is not necessarily a restore point.

The Figma card currently says it will discard later entries, including exported G-code. That conflicts with the recent implementation: commit `076ed1d4c3` saves the current model first, restores the selected model and effective project settings, and records the restore as a new version. Conversation, plan, audit, and print records stay current; exported files and printer activity are untouched. Commit `0dbc454843` also removed the old agent `history_restore` tool.

I’d use this flow:

1. **Timeline row:** a quiet “Model version saved · 13:04” label with a **Restore…** action. Keep it out of ordinary message rows.
2. **Confirmation:** “Restore the model and project settings from 13:04?” Then two short sections: **Changes:** model and effective project settings. **Stays:** conversation, plan, print records, exported files, and the current model as a recoverable version.
3. **Actions:** **Cancel** and **Restore model**. Remove the blank outlined button.
4. **Afterward:** show a restore event in the timeline with a link to Version history, and prompt the user to review the retained plan and slice again before printing.

This fits the current [restore code](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectAutosave.cpp:968) and [confirmation flow](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/StatusRow.cpp:494). The key design change is to present restoration as a **new, recoverable model state**, not deletion of the conversation below a point in time.

## My request:
Use wordking "Revert to here". it is easier for users to understand. but we don't want this to occupy such a big space, Because this will be associated with every change. 

I believe a common practice here is to have a small revert icon as the flag for such action. Mouse hovering world show "Revert to here" popover. Then when user clicked that icon, it'll expand into a full size explanation for what will happen, and a 'confirm" and "cancel" vbutton. Check your knowledge or online, especially other chat app, to see if this is the common knowledge and if it is, where or the where do those apps typically place the small revert icon?

I’ll check how current chat and coding assistants place rollback controls in message history, then map that pattern onto the timeline frame. I’ll keep “Revert to here” as the action label and focus on a compact control that can repeat beside many changes.

The examples support your direction, with one important distinction: Cursor puts restore on a hovered earlier message, while Replit attaches rollback to checkpoint entries. Claude Code uses a separate rewind picker. I’m going to recommend a trailing action on each change row, with the full explanation opening only after a click.

Yes—the compact, contextual action is an established pattern, though there isn’t one universal icon or position. [Cursor puts “Restore Checkpoint” at the bottom right of a previous message on hover](https://prod.cursor.com/help/ai-features/agent). [Replit puts “Rollback to here” on the checkpoint entry itself](https://docs.replit.com/features/version-control/checkpoints-and-rollbacks). [Claude Code uses a separate rewind picker](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing).

For JusPrin, I’d put a small **revert arrow at the trailing right edge of each change row**, aligned with its title or timestamp. That ties the action to the exact change without adding height to every entry. I’d avoid the left edge, where the timeline already uses icons to identify what happened.

- **Hover or keyboard focus:** reveal the icon and a text tooltip, **“Revert to here.”**
- **Click:** open an anchored explanation panel with **Cancel** and **Revert to here**. Keep it open until the user chooses; a hover tooltip should not contain buttons. [W3C distinguishes tooltips from interactive popups](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tooltip/).
- **Explanation:** name the selected change and make “here” precise: *the project state after this change*. Say that the current model is saved in Version history, while conversation, exported files, and printer activity remain as they are.

One implementation detail matters: the new [autosave design](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/agent-docs/jusprin/autosave-version-history.md) can combine nearby edits into one version. To offer **Revert to here on every change**, each change row needs an exact saved version ID. Until that link exists, show the icon only on rows with a restorable state; otherwise it could revert to a different point than the row promises.

content.text:
Autosave **checks every 2 seconds**, but it does not create a checkpoint every 2 seconds. It normally saves a model version after edits have been quiet for 1.5 seconds, so nearby edits can become one saved version. Explicit save points also occur around some agent actions. Chat and other document changes can be persisted without creating a new model version. [Autosave scheduling](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectAutosave.cpp:492)

The link uses an **ID, not a timestamp guess**:

1. Each edit gets a sequence number plus its conversation and preceding message or tool ID. [Change recording](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ProjectStateDocument.cpp:1067)
2. A checkpoint records the sequence number of the last change it captured as `changeSeq`. [Checkpoint capture](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/ProjectAutosave.cpp:393)
3. The timeline puts “Revert to here” on the row ending at that sequence number. If several edits were grouped into one save, there is one control after the last included edit. [Timeline rendering](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/components/ChangeRows.tsx:21)

For example, if edits 41–43 are captured together, the checkpoint records `changeSeq: 43`; the control points to that saved state after edit 43. Older checkpoints created before this field was added have no reliable timeline link, so they remain accessible through Version history without a timeline control.
